name: AP Macroeconomics
overview: AP Macroeconomics is an introductory college course on the economy as a whole: measuring output, unemployment, and inflation; the aggregate demand–aggregate supply model; the financial sector and monetary policy; fiscal policy and its long-run effects; economic growth; and open-economy topics such as the balance of payments and exchange rates. The exam is built on cause-and-effect chains and graphs: you must trace how a policy or shock moves through the money market, loanable funds, AD-AS, and foreign exchange markets, and calculate multipliers, real values, and money creation.
examMode: Hybrid digital: multiple-choice in Bluebook; free-response viewed in Bluebook and answered (including graphs) by hand in a paper booklet. Confirm the current format on AP Central.

sections.name: Section I
sections.notes: Many questions require reasoning through a graph or a chain of effects. Arithmetic is designed to be done by hand.

sections.name: Section II
sections.notes: Includes a 10-minute reading period. The long question is worth half of the section score; each short question is worth a quarter. Correctly labeled graphs are required.

skills.name: 1. Principles and Models
skills.description: Define, explain, and apply economic principles and models.

skills.name: 2. Interpretation
skills.description: Interpret an economic situation and predict or explain outcomes.

skills.name: 3. Manipulation
skills.description: Determine the outcome of an economic situation using economic models and calculations.

skills.name: 4. Graphing and Visuals
skills.description: Create and use correctly labeled graphs and visual representations to explain economic outcomes.

scoring.summary: Section I (60 MCQ) is two-thirds of the composite and Section II one-third, converted to 1–5 using cut points set each year. FRQ points are awarded per element: correct labels, correct shifts and new equilibria, correct direction of change, and explanations. Points can be earned for consistent follow-through on an earlier error.

frqTypes.name: Long FRQ
frqTypes.howScored: Multi-part scenario usually requiring an AD-AS graph and at least one other graph (money market, loanable funds, Phillips curve, or foreign exchange). Points for labeled axes and curves, correct shifts, equilibrium changes, policy identification, and explanations.

frqTypes.name: Short FRQ
frqTypes.howScored: Focused on one model or calculation (money multiplier, balance of payments, PPC, Phillips curve). Points for each correct graph element, calculation with work, or explanation.

strategy: Label every graph completely: axes, curves, equilibrium points, and shifts with arrows or new labels (AD₁, Pl₁).
Follow the chain one step at a time: policy → interest rate → investment → AD → output and price level → unemployment.
When asked to 'explain,' state the economic mechanism, not just the direction.
Know which graph uses nominal vs. real interest rates: money market (nominal), loanable funds (real).
Answer exactly the variable asked (real GDP vs. nominal GDP, price level vs. inflation rate).
Show work for calculations; the arithmetic is simple by design.
Use the 10-minute reading period to sketch graphs and plan chains of effects.
Don't contradict yourself; a correct answer followed by a wrong one may lose the point.
pitfalls: Confusing a change in demand (curve shift) with a change in quantity demanded (movement along).
Saying the Fed controls the federal funds rate directly instead of using tools such as interest on reserves or open-market operations.
Mixing up the spending multiplier (1/MPS) with the tax multiplier (−MPC/MPS).
Shifting LRAS in response to demand shocks.
Confusing currency appreciation with depreciation and their effect on net exports.
Putting the nominal interest rate on the loanable funds graph.
Saying expansionary fiscal policy decreases the deficit.
Forgetting that the short-run Phillips curve shifts with inflation expectations.
referenceSheet: No formula sheet. Know: GDP = C + I + G + Xn; spending multiplier = 1/MPS = 1/(1 − MPC); tax multiplier = −MPC/MPS; real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ (price index/100); inflation = (CPI₂ − CPI₁)/CPI₁ × 100; unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labor force × 100; real interest rate = nominal − expected inflation; money multiplier = 1/reserve requirement; quantity theory MV = PY.

caveats: The Federal Reserve now operates with ample reserves, and the CED emphasizes administered rates (interest on reserves) as the main policy tool; older materials emphasize open-market operations and the reserve requirement.
Cutoffs are estimates; College Board does not publish exact cut scores.
